distractors: To dispute a claim by putting contrary evidence in front of the room and letting the numbers do the work.
To overstate how important something is so that it gets attention it would not otherwise be given, which costs you credibility the second time.

To withdraw public support from a person or a project you previously backed. It is a change of position rather than a choice of words, and the absence of the endorsement is noticed more than any sentence would have been.

To circulate information you know to be untrue in order to damage someone, which is a question about the facts rather than about the tone. It is also the version of this that ends up involving a lawyer.

To pin responsibility for a collective failure on one named person so that the review can be closed and everyone else can get back to work. It is usually done without malice and it is almost always the wrong answer, because the conditions that produced the failure are still there for whoever fills the seat next.
